explanation:
## How the puzzle works

**What the grids contain.** Each input is a black (0) background with several solid rectangles of colour 1. The output keeps every rectangle in the same place but paints it with concentric rings.

**The ring colours.** Give each cell of a rectangle a *depth*: its distance to the nearest edge of the rectangle, `min(y−y0, y1−y, x−x0, x1−x)`.
- Depth 0, the outer border, stays colour 1.
- Depth 1 becomes 2.
- Depth 2 becomes 3.
- Depth 3 becomes 2 again. You can see this in the centre cells of the 7×8 rectangle in pair 1 and the 8×8 rectangle in pair 3.

So after the border, the colours alternate 2, 3, 2, 3, … going inward. A depth-4 cell never appears in the train pairs, so I continue the alternation, which is the simplest choice. The tables below show this explains every rectangle:

| Rectangle | Depths present | Painted colours |
|---|---|---|
| Pair 1, 3×3 | 0, 1 | 1, 2 |
| Pair 2, 4×4 | 0, 1 | 1, 2 |
| Pair 2, 3×3 | 0, 1 | 1, 2 |
| Pair 2, 6×5 | 0, 1, 2 | 1, 2, 3 |
| Pair 3, 5×7 | 0, 1, 2 | 1, 2, 3 |
| Pair 1, 7×8 | 0, 1, 2, 3 | 1, 2, 3, 2 |
| Pair 3, 8×8 | 0, 1, 2, 3 | 1, 2, 3, 2 |

**A trap in the test grid.** In the test input colour 1 outnumbers 0, so a "most common colour" helper would call 1 the background. In every train pair the background is 0 and the shapes are 1. Because of that, I find the rectangles as connected components of non-zero cells instead of using the background helper.

**Applying it to the test.** The test has three rectangles:

| Rectangle | Size | Depths | Painted colours |
|---|---|---|---|
| Top | 6×11 | up to 2 | border 1, ring 2, 3-band core |
| Right | 8×7 | up to 3 | border 1, ring 2, ring 3, 2-coloured centre |
| Left | 3×5 | up to 1 | border 1, 1×3 strip of 2 |

All of these depths occur in the train pairs, so the test needs no guess about deeper rings.

**Construction stages.** The program starts from a copy of the input. It paints one rectangle at a time and emits the canvas after each one, then emits the finished grid.
